title: Catherine of Siena (1347–1380)
hookLine: a dyer's daughter who cared for plague victims and wrote hard letters to popes

cards: Siena, in Italy. A wool dyer's house, smelling of vats and wet cloth, crowded with children and never quiet. Catherine is one of the youngest.
Her parents want her married. She wants to give her whole life to God. So, as a teenager, she cuts off her hair, and her furious family makes her do the housework like a servant.

She doesn't fight them. She decides, she says later, to build a room inside herself where she can always be with God, whatever her hands are doing. This dyer's daughter will end up telling popes what to do.

teach.h: NURSING THE SICK, HOLDING A HEAD.
teach.b: Catherine joined a group of Dominican laywomen who wore the habit but lived at home. For three years she hardly left her little room, praying. Then, she said, she was sent out.
When plague swept Siena, she nursed the sick others were afraid to touch. She walked with a young man condemned to death all the way to the executioner's block, and held his head.

Then came the letters. For most of her life she couldn't write well, so she dictated them, sometimes several at once, to friends taking turns. Hundreds survive, to soldiers, queens, friends and popes.
For decades the popes had lived not in Rome but in Avignon, in France. Catherine thought the pope belonged in Rome, with his flock. So she wrote to Pope Gregory the Eleventh, bluntly and lovingly.
She called him, in Italian, something like sweet daddy, then told him to be a man, stop being afraid, and come back. She even traveled to Avignon to say it to his face. And he did go back to Rome.
She died a few years later, still young.
In 1970 Pope Paul the Sixth named her a Doctor of the Church. Today's line is often quoted as hers: be who God meant you to be and you will set the world on fire. That's a modern paraphrase.

teach.h: IF YOU ARE WHAT YOU SHOULD BE.
teach.b: What she actually wrote to a friend was closer to: if you are what you should be, you'll set all of Italy on fire. Either way, the point is hers.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Catherine of Siena on 29 April; she is a patron of Italy and of Europe, and her letters and her book, the Dialogue, are still read as guides to prayer.

games.q: you're Catherine. the pope is living in France, and you believe he belongs in Rome. you're a dyer's daughter with no title. what do you do?
o: write to him bluntly, then go and tell him to his face.
ask a bishop to raise it someday.
games.why: she wrote him letters, calling him sweet daddy and telling him not to be afraid, then went to Avignon. and he did go back to Rome.

practice: Think of something you've been needing to say to someone: a hard truth, a boundary, a worry about them.

Catherine was blunt, but she wrapped her bluntness in love, so find a first sentence that is kind and true at once, no sarcasm, no speech. If you pray, you can go to her room inside, and ask for courage.
